title: Nasdaq-100 Futures Plunge as Amazon & Intel Shares Dive Post‑Earnings – Live CNBC Updates
body:
Amazon.com Inc. and Intel Corp. sent shockwaves through the tech‑heavy Nasdaq‑100 on Thursday, dragging the index’s futures down 1.7 percent in after‑hours trading. Both companies reported earnings that fell short of analysts’ expectations, prompting sharp sell‑offs in their shares and raising concerns about the pace of growth in two of the market’s most influential sectors—e‑commerce and semiconductors.

Amazon, the world’s largest online retailer, posted a quarterly revenue of $149.2 billion, missing the consensus forecast of $151.1 billion. More worrisome for investors was the company’s net income, which slipped to $1.3 billion from $3.2 billion a year earlier, driven largely by higher logistics costs, a slowdown in advertising spend, and a modest decline in its high‑margin “Amazon Web Services” (AWS) cloud segment. While the firm’s earnings per share (EPS) of $0.21 beat the $0.20 consensus, the revenue miss and muted guidance for the upcoming quarter outweighed the EPS beat, prompting a 5.3 percent decline in Amazon’s stock by the close of regular trading.

Intel, the venerable chipmaker, fared no better. The company reported fourth‑quarter revenue of $15.0 billion, a 2 percent drop from the same period last year and below the $15.4 billion expected by Wall Street. The earnings surprise was even more pronounced on the profit side, with non‑GAAP EPS of $0.34 versus the anticipated $0.46. Intel’s CEO, Pat Gelsinger, cited “ongoing supply chain constraints” and “delayed ramp‑up of its new manufacturing nodes” as primary culprits. The stock slid 6.1 percent, adding further weight to the Nasdaq‑100 futures decline.

The twin earnings disappointments have broader implications for the technology sector, which has been the engine of market gains this year. Analysts point out that Amazon’s slowdown may be an early signal of a cooling consumer‑spending environment, especially as inflationary pressures persist and discretionary income tightens. The company’s advertising revenue—a fast‑growing line item that has become a key profit driver—declined 3 percent year‑over‑year, suggesting that marketers are pulling back on spend amid uncertain economic conditions.

Intel’s woes, meanwhile, highlight the ongoing challenges facing the U.S. semiconductor industry in regaining its footing after a period of intense competition from Asian rivals. The firm’s inability to meet its own production targets for the 7‑nanometer and 10‑nanometer processes underscores the difficulty of scaling advanced node manufacturing, a critical factor for maintaining market share against competitors such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) and Samsung. Moreover, Intel’s guidance for the next quarter, which projects revenue growth of only 1‑2 percent, falls short of the 5‑percent growth many investors had hoped for, raising doubts about the company’s ability to capitalize on the resurgence of demand for data‑center chips.

Market reaction has been swift. Nasdaq‑100 futures, which are heavily weighted toward large‑cap technology names, fell 1.7 percent, erasing roughly $300 billion in market value in a matter of minutes. The broader S&P 500 futures also slipped, though by a more modest 0.8 percent, reflecting the outsized influence of the two stocks on the index’s composition. Fixed‑income markets responded with a modest rise in Treasury yields, as investors sought safety amid the tech‑sector turbulence.

Looking ahead, the next few weeks will be critical for both companies and the broader market. Amazon is expected to release its Q3 earnings next month, and analysts will be watching closely for signs that its advertising business can rebound and that AWS can sustain its high‑margin growth. Intel, on the other hand, has pledged to accelerate its “IDM 2.0” strategy, which includes expanding its own manufacturing capacity and forging new partnerships with third‑party fabs. The success of this plan will hinge on the company’s ability to deliver chips on schedule and to win back key customers in the data‑center and PC markets.

In the meantime, investors are likely to remain cautious, with the Nasdaq‑100’s near‑term trajectory hinging on whether the earnings setbacks are isolated incidents or indicative of a broader slowdown in tech spending. The market’s next move will be shaped by upcoming corporate reports, macroeconomic data on consumer confidence, and the Federal Reserve’s policy outlook, all of which could either reinforce the current bearish tilt or provide the catalyst needed to restore optimism in the sector.
